items.title: Diamond Foundry Presents 200-Mm Single-Crystal Diamonds Wafer
items.author: giuliomagnifico
items.content:
A diamond normally belongs in a jewelry display case, not in a high-performance computer. At least, that was the obvious assumption for a long time. Diamond Foundry aims to change that and says it presented the first continuous single-crystal diamond with a diameter of 200 millimeters on November 5, 2026. This brings the material to a size commonly used in the semiconductor industry. The exceptionally high thermal conductivity of diamond is particularly interesting and could help cool powerful AI accelerators in the long term. However, this is still an unpolished crystal, not a substrate already qualified for mass production.

According to Diamond Foundry, the material presented consists of a single, continuous crystal. Accordingly, it is neither several diamond pieces joined together nor a polycrystalline structure. The company describes the 200-millimeter diameter as a major technological advance. The development was presented in connection with CarbonSemi 2026 in Ningbo, China. CEO Martin Roscheisen presented the result in a video presentation. According to the company, the work stems from research activities by Stefan Gsell and Martin Fischer, who have been working on producing larger single-crystal diamonds for around 25 years. Both joined Diamond Foundry in 2022 through its acquisition of Augsburg Diamond Technology.

The size of the crystal is crucial. Although synthetic diamonds for technical applications have been produced for some time, the available dimensions have so far limited many potential applications. A diameter of 200 millimeters fundamentally opens up the possibility of manufacturing larger technical components from a single crystal. However, whether this can be done economically remains to be demonstrated. Diamond has exceptionally high thermal conductivity. High-purity single crystals can transport heat much faster than many conventional materials used in electronic systems.

Heat dissipation is becoming an increasingly significant technical challenge for modern AI accelerators. Ever more powerful processing units generate considerable power losses over relatively small areas. Local temperature peaks, known as Hotspot peaks, are particularly critical. Diamond could be used here as a heat spreader. The material would not remove heat from the system on its own, but would initially spread it over a larger area. The heat would then still need to be dissipated by heatsinks, liquid cooling, or other cooling systems. This distinction is particularly important. A material with better thermal conductivity does not automatically replace an existing cooling system. However, it could improve thermal conditions inside a processor package.

Diamond is also interesting for specialized applications because of its mechanical properties and electrical insulation. However, the actual benefits depend heavily on purity, crystal defects, surface quality, and integration into the respective assembly. Producing a large crystal is not the same as successfully mass-producing finished components. The material must be further processed for practical use. Depending on the application, this includes precision cutting, grinding, polishing, and surface-quality inspection, among other steps.

Defects in the crystal lattice are particularly problematic in large single crystals. Such defects can impair mechanical, thermal, or electrical properties. It must also be ensured that production can be repeated reliably over extended periods. Diamond Foundry has so far published no verifiable information on production yield, defect densities, or the cost of a finished 200-mm substrate. No specific customer qualifications or firm date for commercial mass production have been announced either. The claim that 300-mm single crystals may also be achievable in the future therefore remains, for now, a technical assessment by the company.

A diameter of 200 millimeters corresponds to the format of classic 8-inch wafers. This format continues to be used in numerous areas of the semiconductor industry, particularly for analog circuits, sensors, and power electronics. However, a diamond substrate cannot simply be used in place of a silicon wafer in existing manufacturing processes. The material properties differ considerably, meaning that many applications would require specialized processing steps. Diamond Foundry is already working to expand its production of technical diamond substrates. Among other things, the company points to a multibillion-euro project in Spain associated with the European Chips Act. Whether the new 200-mm single crystal actually leads to economically competitive products therefore depends on more than the achievable size alone. Manufacturing costs, the quality of the finished surfaces, and industrial availability will be at least as important.

In my view, the 200-mm diamond presented is an interesting material development that extends beyond semiconductor manufacturing alone. The thermal limits of modern high-performance electronics are becoming increasingly relevant, and new materials could help reduce these constraints in the long term. However, the announcement should not already be equated with a revolution in processor cooling. An unpolished crystal is not yet a ready-to-use cooling substrate, and without information on cost, quality, and production volumes, its economic significance remains unclear.

The technological advance is remarkable, provided the manufacturer’s claims can be confirmed. The next development steps will show whether this actually leads to a practical solution for future AI systems.

items.title: D200mm: A New Scale for Single‑Crystal Diamond
items.author: addaon
items.content:
Twenty-five years of scientific pursuit have produced the first-ever single‑crystal diamond measuring 200mm in diameter.

At Diamond Foundry, we have created the first-ever D200mm single‑crystal diamond: one continuous crystal, 200mm in diameter. It marks a fundamental step forward in our ability to manufacture diamond as a technology material at semiconductor scale.

Diamond combines the highest thermal conductivity with exceptional mechanical strength, electrical insulation, optical properties, and the potential for extreme electronic performance. For decades, those properties have pointed toward new possibilities in technology. One basic limitation has stood in the way: size.

Watch CEO Martin Roscheisen’s announcement of D200mm at Carbon Semi 2026:

The semiconductor industry is built around the ability to manufacture extraordinary materials at wafer scale. Silicon’s progression toward larger wafers transformed electronics by allowing increasingly sophisticated devices to be manufactured economically and repeatably.

Diamond has faced a different path. Natural diamond is constrained by geology, while conventional lab‑grown diamond has historically been constrained to relatively small crystal dimensions. As diamond’s properties became increasingly relevant to high‑power electronics, AI computing, optics, and quantum systems, crystal size remained a fundamental bottleneck.

Growing diamond at this scale required advances in plasma physics, reactor engineering, and process control.

Twenty-Five Years of Perseverance

The work behind this milestone began well before Diamond Foundry. Stefan Gsell and Martin Fischer have pursued the scientific and engineering challenge of growing high‑quality single‑crystal diamond of scalable size for 25 years. Stefan and Martin joined Diamond Foundry in 2022 through our acquisition of Augsburg Diamond Technology (Audiatec), bringing their crystal-growth expertise together with our reactor technology and manufacturing capabilities.

“This is one of those milestones that once seemed almost impossible,” said Martin Roscheisen, CEO of Diamond Foundry Inc. “Hundreds of DF engineers, scientists, and technicians contributed to us getting here. It is the accumulated result of countless experiments, failures, inventions, rebuilt machines, and insights over more than a decade.”

“Stefan and Martin pursued this goal for 25 years,” Roscheisen said. “There are very few examples in technology of someone sticking to a really hard scientific challenge with that level of perseverance. They kept going when the prevailing view was that single‑crystal diamond simply could not be made at this scale. Today, the perseverance shows as the first-ever D200mm single‑crystal diamond. And best of all, it makes D300mm predictable as well.”

That perseverance is reflected in advances across plasma generation, growth chemistry, reactor architecture, crystal engineering, thermal management, metrology, automation, and manufacturing.

What This Means for Computing

For us, D200mm is part of a broader effort to turn single‑crystal diamond from a scarce material measured in gemstones into a tech‑industrial semiconductor substrate manufactured at scale.

That matters as computing systems encounter increasingly severe thermal constraints. Modern AI processors concentrate enormous amounts of power into microscopic regions of silicon. Diamond’s exceptional thermal conductivity can spread that heat at the material level, creating new possibilities for chip architectures, power densities, reliability, and cooling.

A Beginning for Wafer‑Scale Diamond

We are developing single‑crystal diamond for semiconductor and advanced‑technology applications where its combination of thermal, mechanical, electrical, and optical properties can enable performance beyond the limits of conventional materials. D200mm demonstrates a path beyond the size limitation that has held diamond back.

“Technology history is often written around the moment something finally works,” Roscheisen said. “But that moment rests on the people who were willing to spend years, sometimes decades, making it work. This diamond exists because hundreds of people contributed, and because a few people refused to give up on the idea for 25 years.”

Single‑crystal diamond has entered the wafer‑scale era.

items.title: Crystal 1.22
items.author: ksec
items.content:
We are announcing a new Crystal release 1.22.0 with several new features and bug fixes.

This release includes 251 changes since 1.21.1 by 33 contributors. We thank all the contributors for all the effort put into improving the language! ❤️

Below we list the most remarkable changes in the language, compiler, and stdlib. For more details, visit the full changelog.

Crystal processes exit immediately when writing to STDOUT or STDERR fails with . This closely resembles the default behaviour of the signal. Previously, the failing write would raise , which typically prints an error message and exits. This error message is now removed (#17335).

You can opt out of this behaviour with STDOUT.exit_on_broken_pipe = false.

Constants can have type declarations (#16951). They work exactly as you would expect the combination of constants and type declarations to be.

The targets and moved from Tier 2 to Tier 1. The only missing piece was that we were lacking official builds, but we have that since 1.19.

had been deprecated sine before 1.0 and now we finally removed it (#17367)

  • New macros enable more text operations at compile time: (#17176), (#17169) and supports (#17170)

New constants and provide access to the compile time flags (#17392).

We completely revamped DWARF parsing to enhance performance and reduce memory usage. The DWARF parser now scans sections on demand (#17283) and builds an efficient index table once (#17410, #17455), which results in blazingly fast look ups. Decoded backtrace lines are cached in an LRU cache (#17285).

Also added aupport for DWARF 5 features and (#17445).

We merged numerous improvements and bug fixes for HTTP.

  • and moved from to (#17196)
  • Add (#17326)
  • Serialize in HTTP body with header (#17388)
  • Reject unrecognized HTTP header (#17140), invalid (#17262), and invalid HTTP trailer (#17337)
  • Fix the return values of and (#17257, #17273)
  • Fix HTTP.parse_headers_and_body to not raise with (#17272)
  • Close on during request (#17318)
  • Fix Content-Encoding: deflate (#17261)
  • Fix parsing empty header name (#17254)
  • Fix HTTP::Request#form_params? to ignore invalid content-type (#17256)

All targets support a native event loop based directly on the system selector and use it by default.

We enabled on Solaris (#17370) and on all remaining BSD targets (#17421, #17420). is still available as a fallback, but now it’s strictly opt-in and becoming technically obsolete. We expect to deprecate in a following release.

We finally enabled support for Kernel TLS in the OpenSSL bindings by default (#17059)

This was reverted in 1.22.1 and will stay disabled.

  • (#17307), as well as , , now receive a argument(#17391)
  • Add (#17428)
  • Add Time::Span#to_nanoseconds etc. (#17190)
  • Fixed backtraces when linking with on musl-libc (#17316)
  • Uppercase instance and class variables (#17160)
  • HTTP::Request#local_address and (#17260)
  • and (#17494)
  • Support for LLVM 23.1 and 24.0 (#17432)

Updated distribution-scripts (#17178) brings upgrades of package dependencies, docker base images etc.

This is the first release featuring builds for .

Crystal established a forward compatibility policy in RFC 30: Building Crystal 1.22 requires a stage-0 compiler at 1.14 or higher.

We have been able to do all of this thanks to the continued support of 84codes and all other sponsors. To maintain and increase the development pace, donations, and sponsorships are essential. OpenCollective is available for that.

Reach out to crystal@manas.tech if you’d like to become a direct sponsor or find other ways to support Crystal. We thank you in advance!
